name: Ute Creek SWCD
title: Canadian River Noxious Weed Treatment
summary: Hand Treatment, Cut Stump and Chemical Treatment of Siberian Elm, Saltcedar and Musk Thistle will be performed along the Canadian River Watershed partnering with US Forest Service and the Canadian River Riparian Restoration Project. The project is within an area that was previously treated by aerial application of herbicide using a helicopter equipped with GPS applying Amazapere to remove Saltcedar (which is not effective in the treatment of Siberian Elm); this follow up treatment using Cut Stump method and applying Garlon 4 (Triclopyr) to Elm and resprouts of Saltcedar and using Milestone (Amenopyralid) to treat Musk Thistle. The Canadian River Noxious Weed Treatment is a small portion of a larger watershed scale project which includes 8 Soil and Water Conservation Districts working together under a Joint Powers Agreement plus 21 state and federal agencies.

name: Salado Soil and Water Conservation District
title: Initial Noxious Weed Mapping
summary: This project will be the first on its kind. Salado has no noxious weed mapping of any kind. This project is designed to map all the acres included in the boundaries of the soil and water conservation district. The contractor will contact landowners and explain the project, receive permission to map their land. Mark the noxious weeds, give a summary to the landowner and keep an updated electronic map. The project will be scheduled to begin January with the contractor contacting the landowners for permissions. February thru May will be the actual mapping. June will be the final report and completion of the project.

name: Quemado SWCD
title: Initial Noxious Weed Mapping
summary: Quemado has no noxious weed mapping of any kind. This project is designed to map all the acres included in the boundaries of the soil and water conservation district. The contractor and the district employee will contact landowners and explain the project. At this time permission to map their land will be acquired. Mark the noxious weeds, give a summary to the landowner and keep an updated electronic map. The project will be scheduled to begin January with the contacting of landowners. February thru May will be the actual mapping. June will be the final report and completion of the project.

name: Socorro Soil & Water Conservation District
title: Socorro SWCD Holmes Property Continuing Habitat Restoration
summary: The Holmes property is on the East Side of the Rio Grande, directly across the river from Socorro, NM.  The property is bordered on the north by NMDGF land, and on the south by BLM (public) land.  This site is a popular place for local residents to sightsee, photograph, hunt, fish and enjoy easy access to the Rio Grande, made possible by the large arroyo running through the middle of it, and, more importantly, Mr. Holmes' desire to keep the land fully accessible.  Although it is his private land, he has allowed NMDGF to install signage, and he even installed a non-locking gate to ease access.  In 2007, the Socorro SWCD, using NMERD funding and state funding, contracted for 20.2 acres of non-native phreatophyte extraction and mulching.  Due to the infestation level, this left little vegetation remaining, save a small grove of old growth Rio Grande Cottonwood.  Following 7,220' of fencing, we planted 100 Rio Grande Cottonwood and Goodding's Black Willow trees, 250 assorted native shrubs, and broadcast 250 pounds of native grass seed.  The poles and shrub planting was aided by a soil salinity survey, helping us target the best spots for revegetation.  Following a wildfire in 2023, the property is now in need of fence repair, noxious species treatment, and further planting.

name: Sierra Soil and Water Conservation District
title: Tiffany Basin Saltcedar Resprout Treatment
summary: To continue efforts towards restoration of riparian habitat impacted by the June 2017 Tiffany Fire, near San Marcial in Socorro County, Sierra SWCD, NM Ranch Properties, the Save Our Bosque Task Force, and New Mexico State Forestry have been working together to control noxious Saltcedar that became prevalent within the burn scar. Over the years since the fire, Saltcedar has been mechanically treated using grant dollars provided by various agencies including Water Trust Board and NM State Forestry. Mechanical treatment consisted of one of two methods: (1) mowing standing Saltcedar or (2) extracting Saltcedar with an excavator and mulching/spreading slash material. Areas that were mowed resulted in an increased number of resprouts compared to areas that were extracted. However, some locations within the project area could not be reached by any type of machinery due the number of down cottonwood skeletons caused by the fire. We plan to conduct a foliar application of herbicide during late September through early October. The selected contractor, will use an adaptive mixture of ground and aerial drone herbicide application. We would like to see continuous areas where harmful noxious weeds have been removed, allowing more desirable native plants to establish and thrive, thus restoring valuable riparian habitat. Sierra SWCD will host an education and outreach presentation that landowner and agency personnel will be invited to attend where they can see drone herbicide application and discuss the importance of responsibly treating noxious weeds.

name: Santa Clara Pueblo
title: Santa Clara Pueblo Invasive Plant Species Management Plan
summary:
The management and control of invasive species on Santa Clara Pueblo lands is a deemed priority and the Pueblo has already acquired and spent millions of dollars restoring riparian areas along the Rio Grande and Santa Clara Creek to protect riparian and wetland resources. Control efforts in other locations including agricultural fields along the Rio Grande have made a substantial difference. Although most large invasives have been removed, resprouting continues and the agricultural habitats need routine work to keep up with and improve the progress already made. 
For weed management on Santa Clara Pueblo, water stations include large capacity storage, pressurized systems, and underbody sprayers to be used at reducing invasive species spread and would ultimately save land managers hours of time for invasive weed removal. The timeline for our project begins in September of 2024 and will include seasonal weed removal activities 2 to 3 times throughout the fall and winter and early spring months which will conclude prior to June 30th, 2025. The Santa Clara Pueblo Department of Agriculture and Department of Forestry will be completing the field work within the areas of Santa Clara Pueblo.

name: Colfax Soil and Water Conservation District
title: White Peak Landscape Invasive Thistle Mapping and Treatment
summary:
Since 2007 the White Peak Landscape has been a focal area for forest restoration and fuels reduction, managed by the New Mexico State Land Office (NMSLO). Active forest management including forest thinning, prescribed fire, and removal of forest products have been essential to increasing ecosystem resilience to wildfire and reduce detrimental impacts of wildfire to the surrounding communities and watershed. Canada thistle has been persistent in presence and spread despite a robust native vegetation response following forest management activities. These noxious weeds have hindered the recovery of native species. While native vegetation is well adapted to frequent, low intensity fire at the project area, the presence of non-native, noxious plants shifts the competitive balance and creates a more undesirable understory composition following prescribed fires. 
NMSLO proposes to integrate yearly surveys and herbicide treatments into forest management activities. Over five years NMSLO will perform an annual pedestrian survey to detect and map occurrences of noxious weeds. Funds made available from this grant will help to provide the first year of treatments and mapping, kicking off a five-year total effort from NMSLO. Herbicide applications would be applied to targeted noxious species, with a focus on Canada thistle (Cirsium arvense), as well as musk thistle (Carduus nutans), Scotch thistle (Onopordum acanthium), and bull thistle (Cirsium vulgare). After a period of five years following effective treatments, management will shift, prioritizing early detection and treatment of subsequent occurrences. Following new forest management treatments,  heightened awareness and survey would take place for that specific treatment unit.

name: Boy Scouts of America - Philmont Scout Ranch
title: Crater Lake Noxious Weed Treatment
summary:
Philmont Scout Ranch has a long-standing history of doing responsible and effective land management which includes extensive work with the Colfax County Soil and Water Conservation District to combat noxious weeds on Philmont Scout Ranch, Vermejo Park Ranch and the Valle Vidal. 

Over the past 13 years, Philmont has undertaken significant efforts to inventory and treat noxious weeds, employing extensive chemical, manual and biological control methods. This grant will enable Philmont to further treat acres of noxious weeds which complements previous efforts and ongoing projects. Since 2023, Philmont has initiated restorative thinning plans in two units on the ranch covering a total of 900 acres. Within the Crater Restorative Thinning Unit ground disturbance from machinery has primed the area for higher-than-normal infestation of noxious weeds. Within the treatment unit there is a vast road and trail network along with stream channels that all can act as a mode for seed to rapidly disperse and move into other areas of lesser concern.  As part of a holistic land management approach, this project will address the need for treatment of know species in the unit (musk, bull and scotch thistle) and implement EDRR (hoary cress, yellow toadflax and canada thistle).  

The project area covers 420 acres in total which has been under ongoing treatment of noxious weeds for the past three years. Utilizing seasonal staff for herbicide treatments and conducting mechanical removal workdays with volunteer labor. A contract sprayer will be utilized to effectively treat the extensive acreage in this unit.

name: Otero Soil and Water Conservation District
title: Precision Weed Mapping in Otero County
summary: Otero Soil and Water Conservation District has a very active Noxious Weed Management Program.  The only component we do not have the staffing for is the surveying/mapping of populations. We plan to change that by hiring a contractor to map African Rue utilizing a drone.  In September we will do the contracting so that the work can begin immediately while African Rue is active before the fall treatment window.  This will help us pinpoint any satellite locations for treatment.  An ongoing contract with the Bureau of Land Management will cover the cost of treatment in October.  We anticipate a minimum of 7,500 acres to be mapped this fall. African Rue will be dormant in the winter before it reappears in early spring.  Any acres remaining will be mapped in the spring.

name: Chaves Soil and Water Conservation District
title: Control of Noxious Weeds in Chaves County
summary: The focus of this project will focus on mechanical treatment in combination with chemical or herbicide treatments. The target species will be African Rue, Russian Knapweed, Salt Cedar and Scotch Thistle. Mapped African Rue populations have been treated with herbicide treatments and will continue to be treated by herbicides. Russian Knapweed has already been extensively mapped and with locations being numerous, the focus will be on mapping Salt cedar. Scotch Thistle has a concentrated population. The focus will be on preventing the plant from spreading and detecting any other population(s). The key to control of Russian Knapweed is to continuously stress it. Combination treatments of mechanical treatments (mastication), cultural (planting native species), and chemical (herbicide treatment) have been shown to have the best results on this species. Monitoring before and after treatment will determine how effective the treatments have been. Salt Cedar will be a challenge as cut-stump treatment is the preferred method. The preferred method to treat Salt Cedar is a combination treatment of chemical and mechanical treatment. All treatments will be monitored before and after implementation of methods mentioned above. Funding will go towards cut-stump treatment, herbicide application, and planting native species (native grass seed mix).

name: Carlsbad Soil and Water Conservation District
title: African Rue Treatment in southeastern New Mexico
summary: Southeast NM is seeing a large uptick in the spread of African Rue due to the movement of the oilfield industry. Carlsbad SWCD is the lead for the Eddy County Coordinated Weed Management  Group. We work with BLM, Eddy County, City of Carlsbad, Carlsbad Irrigation District, Oil and Gas Industry and numerous other agencies. We will apply herbicide by hand treatment method to African Rue.  Optimal treatment of African Rue is twice a year, in the spring and again in the fall when the plant is blooming.

name: New Mexico Wilderness Alliance (New Mexico Wild)
title: Gila Wilderness- Invasive Species Field Team
summary: In recent years the Gila National Forest (GNF) has been working with partner groups to complete invasive species surveys of the Wilderness areas it manages. 512 survey miles were completed in the Gila by partner group, Heart of the Gila. This project will use results of these surveys to target noxious weed treatments primarily in the Gila Wilderness. New Mexico Wild staff will be trained in Invasive species identification and physical removal methods. Focus species include Class A (yellow toadflax, camelthorn), Class B (bull thistle, poison hemlock), Class C (Siberian Elm, Eurasian watermilfoil, cheat grass).  Priorities will be identified with the GNF in early Spring, 2025, training begins in April, and five multiday backcountry hitches to conduct treatments will take place subsequently. The team will locate previous, spatially mapped infestations of Class A, B, and C species and complete treatments using established physical removal methods. If new infestations are found, they will be immediately surveyed with the Forest Service TESP-IS mobile application and then removed in an EDRR protocol. New infestations that can’t be immediately treated will be mapped. We will follow removal, EDRR, and survey guidelines laid out by USDA Forest Service-Southwestern region. The project also includes an education component consisting of four projects open to volunteers, who will help remove priority invasives. These projects will include sharing information from NMDA about detecting and treating early infestations of invasive plants, plus information about identifying priority noxious weeds. Post evaluation of treatments will be conducted by the GNF and partners.

name: Border Soil & Water Conservation District
title: Leave the Lands Better Than You Found Them Through Noxious Weed Management
summary:
Our 18-month proposal for Class B species focuses on African Rue, Spiny cockleburs and thistles.  Eighteen months can provide three Rue treatments; it is sprayed when in bloom in spring and fall.  The third treatment can take place September 2025.
Objectives and methods include:  
1) Land manager permissions are in progress.  Landowner information will be continually updated through Chaves and Roosevelt County Assessors and onX mapping application.  Written agreements, JPAs and MOUs will be offered to land managers.  
2) Mapping & Education:  Provide trainings and materials to include, plant identification, detection and reporting of infestations using GPS, onX, Avenza and ArcGIS mapping.  Update existing maps as infestations are located and provide detailed treatment and reclamation data.  Coordinate with Extension Services to offer CEUs and herbicide application trainings.  
3) Integrate treatment plans:  Offer treatment cost-shares particularly for initial Rue treatment in September 2024.  Procurement procedures in place by October 2024 to complete RFPs enabling commercial applicator availability.  More applicators are now available in the area and have expressed interest in BSWCD’s Noxious Weed Program.
5) Establish reclamation plans:  Continuously monitor treated areas for timely reclamation practices. Offer cost-sharing for native seed, appropriate soil preparation materials like fertilizer and compost materials.  Documentation, photos, data sharing and on-site visits will be ongoing.
6) Strengthen partnerships:  Mapping, data sharing and treatments require statewide collaboration with agencies, SWCDs and CWMAs.  Our ultimate objective of landscape restoration naturally encourages teamwork.

name: Taos Land Trust
title: Rio Fernando Park and Vigil y Romo Acequia Invasive Species Mitigation
summary: Taos Land Trust owns and maintains for public use a 20 acre park in Taos, adjacent to a 20 acre Taos municipal open space. We are active parciantes on the Vigil y Romo Acequia, which includes the Town of Taos and adjacent property owners of 5 additional acres in the project area. We will map, immediately address, and treat Class A, Class B, and Class C species that are prevalent on our property and adjacent sites for a total project area of 45 acres. We have begun mapping for Class A, Class B , and Class C species with a seasonal youth crew, and will augment that with mapping using staff time and GPS. For each species, we will identify two 30m X 30m plots with 3m X 3m subplots to monitor pre-and-post treatment inventory. Treatment methods include physical, mechanical, cultural, fire with individual blow torch applications, and chemical with high strength vinegar application. Commercial pesticides will not be used because we will be treating in an 8 acre wetlands area and 20 acres of the site is under a conservation easement. We will host public workshops to share our treatment results. For Siberian elm and Russian olive trees >10 inches, we will mill suitable material for use on the property, as a means to demonstrate possible commercial and artisanal uses for these woods. Work will take place between September 2024 and June 2025. Partners include the Town of Taos, Taos Land Trust, and the Vigil y Romo Acequia commission.

name: Deming Soil & Water Conservation District
title: Luna County Intergrated Weed Management
summary:
Luna County and the Deming Soil and Water Conservation District are concerned with the current infestations of African Rue, Malta Starthistle, Russian Knapweed, and Saltcedar within our county. These noxious and invasive plants reduce the agricultural, economical, and recreational value of the land.   Private landowners, public land users, and local governments and organizations must work together to implement this plan.

In order to achieve our goals, we will be utilizing an experienced contractor to treat these noxious species on public and private land.  Areas of high use will be targeted to reduce the spread of these plants from high volume vehicle and foot traffic.  There will be a strong focus on the treatment of roadways, right of ways, and public areas.  We will be monitoring the acres treated by evaluating current and past treatment areas and identifying areas of infestation that will require future herbicidal applications.

Our goal is to treat the noxious vegetation with herbicides on approximately 350 acres of private and public lands for the period of 9/24 – 11/25.  We will be monitoring these areas for re-infestation and treatment success. Documentation of methods and specific herbicides utilized are required of any contractor or individual who is applying the chemical treatment.  Specific location data (GPS coordinates) will also be required which will enable us to track areas of treatment and possible future reapplication.  Photos of these locations will be taken before and after chemical application to ensure that treatment efforts have been successful.

name: Coddington Twin Springs Ranch
title: Comprehensive Thistle Management Initiative at The Coddington Twin Springs Ranch
summary: We seek support to manage invasive thistles impacting our grasslands through mechanical, chemical, and manual treatments, while also engaging neighboring landowners—many of whom are elderly or infirm—in outreach and education to promote long-term, community-based weed management.

name: San Luis Cabezon Mutual Domesti Water Association
title: Noxious Weed Management along the RIo Puerco
summary:
Grazing: Can be used with some species to reduce seed production, but often needs to be combined with other methods
Mulching: Creates a barrier to weed growth, preventing seeds from germinating

name: Upper Hondo SWCD
title: Community Walk Path Noxious Weed Project
summary: Community walk path needs bi-annual chemical treatment for noxious and invasive weeds. This area is well used by the community as well as students. We are in need of an ATV boom sprayer and chemical to effectively treat this area.

name: Carlsbad Soil and Water Conservation District
title: African Rue Mapping & Management Project
summary: This project aims to improve the mapping and the treatment efficiency of African rue. Our goals for the project are to collect data on infestations, adjust treatment timing, increase treatment efficiency, measure results, and share management resources with our partners.

name: SW Quay SWCD
title: Sustainable Noxious Weed Management for Enhanced Agricultural Productivity
summary: This project focuses on controlling noxious weeds on agricultural land using either mechanical or chemical treatments. By collaborating with producers, we aim to reduce weed populations, improve land productivity, and provide sustainable land management solutions.

name: Mesa Soil & Water Conservation District
title: Mesa SWCD Noxious Weed Treatment
summary: Hand treatment by cut stump method of Siberian Elm and chemical treatment of Saltcedar on the Canadian River. This project is an ongoing effort to restore the Canadian River watershed partnering with landowners, state and federal Agencies and 8 Districts.

name: High Plains Cooperative Weed Management Area
title: Partnering for Noxious Weed Management
summary: All 5 selected activities will be incorporated and all weed classes will be addressed with a focus on African Rue.  Our current Integrated Weed Management project will move forward by leveraging partnerships, developing capacity and expanding education.

name: Colfax Soil And Water Conservation District
title: Black Lake Invasive Thistle Mapping and Treatment
summary: Colfax SWCD proposes mapping and treatment of noxious thistle across 450 acres near Black Lake, NM. Rocky Mountain Ecology (RME) would implement project activities and has successfully teamed with both the NMSLO and CSWCD in the past.

name: New Mexico Wilderness Alliance (New Mexico Wild)
title: Gila Wilderness- Invasive Species Field Team
summary: New Mexico Wild will expand a current project that uses previously mapped infestations to target noxious weeds on the Gila NF for physical removal. We’ll expand the project’s current footprint and increase efficacy of previous treatments with monitoring and re-treatments.

name: Otero Soil and Water Conservation District
title: Precision Ag Mapping of African Rue
summary: Otero SWCD has added drone mapping to our noxious weed management program.  Additional funding is required to adequately map the African Rue populations within Otero County.

name: Central Curry SWCD
title: Sustainable Noxious Weed Management for Enhanced Agricultural Productivity
summary: This project focuses on controlling noxious weeds on agricultural land using either mechanical or chemical treatments. By collaborating with producers, we aim to reduce weed populations, improve land productivity, and provide sustainable land management solutions.

name: Taos Soil and Water Conservation District
title: Mechanical Removal and Follow Up Treatment for Russian Olives In Taos County
summary: This project will focus on mechanical removal of Russian Olive trees on Taos County private agricultural land and follow up treatments to address tree resprouting.

name: Santa Clara Pueblo Forestry
title: Santa Clara Pueblo Invasive Plant Species Management
summary:
The project proposes to do a variety of invasive species planning, prevention, and 
implementation activities on Santa Clara Pueblo lands in conjunction with our newly developed Santa Clara Pueblo 
Invasive Species Management Plan.

name: New Mexico State University
title: Integration of biological control beetles and mowing for improved tamarisk (saltcedar) management.
summary: We propose integrating use of mowing and existing biological control agents (tamarisk leaf beetles) to reduce populations of tamarisk (saltcedar) at Caballo Reservoir. Green leaf volatiles (GLV) will be used to improve tamarisk leaf beetle efficacy.

name: Chaves Soil & Water Conservation District
title: Chaves SWCD Salt Cedar Initiative and Noxious Weed Control
summary: Salt Cedar has infested riparian habitats and is spreading across our waterways, drainages and native grasslands. This initiative will build off previous salt cedar eradication efforts and include monitoring efforts and outreach with public/ stakeholders to collectively address the issue.

name: Cuba Soil and Water Conservation District
title: Cuba SWCD Noxious Weeds
summary: We will use funding to hire contractors for spraying, covering landowner costs for up to 100 acres, instead of employing one person. This approach maximizes efficiency and impact. Targeted noxious weeds are hoary cress, Russian knapweed, thistle, and others.

name: City of Belen
title: Belen Noxious Weed Management
summary: Roadrunner Public Health will provide public health noxious weed vegetation services for pre and post emergent treatment to clear weeds and reduce mosquito harborage targeting both Winter and Summer weeds on City property and right of way.

name: Colfax Soil And Water Conservation District
title: Colfax county / Springer community ditches and Lazy S ranch land -- Integrated Weed  Management (on the ground treatments)
summary:
Integrated weed management along Springer community ditch system--approximately 97.23 acres
Integrated weed management within Lazy S ranch (northern Colfax county)--40 acres

name: Taos Land Trust
title: Rio Fernando Park and Vigil y Romo Acequia Invasive Species Mitigation Phase 2
summary: Building on information from phase 1 of mapping, treatment, and pre/post assessments, we prioritize physical and cultural treatments and conduct additional public workshops on the threat of noxious weeds to productive lands, while leveraging other funds to re-establish  soil health.

name: Ancestral Lands Conservation Corps, a program of Conservation Legacy
title: Tribal Riparian and Forestry Restoration of the Bosque
summary: Ancestral Lands Conservation Corps will partner with the Pueblo of Sandia to address critical conservation needs along the Bosque, treating priority invasive woody species that have severe negative impacts on the health of the Rio Grande and its surrounding forest.
